_transcription: PAGE MAP: the booklet is 15 rendered pages (idx 0-14 = printed folios 1-15), every one accounted for. idx 0 = bilingual cover (Series AABB1/2, SET-1, Q.P. Code 57/2/1, BIOLOGY (Theory), 2 hours, 35 marks, 15 printed pages, 13 questions). ENGLISH = the EVEN indices 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 (folios 3-15). HINDI = the ODD indices 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13. The tops of all seven odd indices open in Hindi (idx 1 Hindi instructions and Q1-3, idx 3 Hindi Q4, idx 5 Hindi Q6(b), idx 7 Hindi Q10, idx 9 Hindi Section C / Q13(a), idx 11 Hindi Q13(b) passage, idx 13 Hindi Q13(b) sub-parts), so no English overflow onto an odd page and no parity inversion; idx 14 (the last page) is English, carrying Q13(b) (i)-(iii). The paper has a text layer (born-digital), but it drops whole lines (Q2's quoted sentence, Q3(a)(i), Q6(b)(ii), Q8(a), Q10(a), Q12's middle, half of the Q13(b) passage), so every row was read off the full-size page by vision; the text layer was used only to confirm the raised decimal dot (U+00B7 in '2·5', written \(2{\cdot}5\)). Structure as printed: Section A Q1-6 @2, Section B Q7-12 @3, Section C Q13 case-based @5 = 35. Instruction (vii) says internal choices exist but gives no count; the roster was built from the scheme's four bare ORs and each confirmed against a printed OR on the paper: Q3, Q6, Q10 and Q13 (four alternatives). Q13(a) is a case study with five 1-mark sub-parts (printed '5x1=5'), one row each. Its OR, Q13(b), replaces the WHOLE case study with a DIFFERENT case study (an RNAi passage and its own bar graph, sub-parts (i)-(iii), scheme split 2/2/1), so it is ONE row Q13b, alternative to Q13ai, with its own passage in context and its own setId (CS2). Quotes straightened (Q2, Q10(a) and Q13(a)(v) print curly double quotes), scientific names plain (Plasmodium, Anopheles, Cynomolgus, E. coli). Kept as printed: Q13(b) 'bicontrol agent', 'monkeys were given', 'control .', Q3(a) 'i.e.,'. Q4's en dash after 'Biogas plants' kept as printed. One question asks the student to draw (Q13(a)(iv), pBR322), so one _drawFigure.

questions.stem: Though filariasis is not fatal, but the disease in humans is responsible for considerable suffering, gross deformities and disability. Write the scientific name of any two helminth worms causing the disease and state two chronic manifestations of filariasis.
"Curd is easier to digest by humans than milk." Justify, giving two suitable reasons.

A person suffering from AIDS dies of opportunistic infections (ARC) i.e., infections that could have been otherwise overcome.
(i) State one reason as to why an 'HIV' patient dies of 'opportunistic infections'.
(ii) Give the scientific name of one bacterium and one parasite which mainly attack a person suffering from AIDS.
(iii) Write the full form of the name of the widely used diagnostic test for AIDS.

In spite of the statutory warning on cigarette packets against 'smoking' and its injurious effects on health, smoking is still prevalent in the society. Enumerate four important health hazards to a smoker.

Study the given diagrams of Biogas plants – 'A' and 'B' and answer the questions that follow :
Which one of the two biogas plants can be used for generating gas fuel and electricity and why ? Give suitable reasons in support of your answer.
questions._figure: REQUIRED: two side-by-side drawings captioned Biogas Plant (A) and Biogas Plant (B), each an inlet box feeding a digester tank, with a gas holder and gas pipe on top and an outlet to a box marked Sludge. The two drawings differ only in the slurry label printed above the inlet box, which is the whole discriminator of the question, so which slurry feeds which plant is withheld here. Page idx 4.

questions.subtopic: Responses to Abiotic Factors and Adaptations
questions._flag: SUBTOPIC GAP: the question is on physiological adaptation of an organism to its abiotic environment (the kangaroo rat's water economy), which was NCERT's 'Organism and its Environment' / 'Adaptations' section, removed by the rationalised syllabus. No live subtopic of Organisms and Populations covers it; filed on the nearest, 'Life History Variation' (populations evolving to maximise fitness in their habitat). The subtopic I would have wanted: 'Adaptations'.
questions.stem: Explain the two physiological attributes which enable a kangaroo rat to survive in desert conditions.

questions.subtopic: Species Numbers and Patterns of Biodiversity
questions._flag: Conditional marking note in the scheme, not a void: 'Note : 1/2 mark to be awarded if student writes either one or both parts correctly in 6(a)(i)'.
questions.stem:
Study the given graphs (X) and (Y) depicting the annual variation in solar radiation on Earth from January to December and answer the undermentioned questions.
(i) Identify the graph that depicts (I) tropical region, and (II) temperate region, respectively.
(ii) Which of the two regions, (X) or (Y), will show high biological diversity and why ? Give two reasons.
questions._figure: REQUIRED: two graphs labelled (X) and (Y), each of Solar radiation (y, arrow upward) against Months from Jan. to Dec. (x, twelve ticks), each with a dashed horizontal reference line and one solid curve. The shape of each curve (how much the radiation varies over the year) is exactly what decides which graph is tropical and which temperate, so it is withheld here. Page idx 4.

questions.stem:
(i) When prickly pear cactus was introduced into Australia in early 1920s, it caused havoc and ecosystem instability by achieving very high population densities. Explain the reason for its rapid spread into millions of hectares of rangeland.
(ii) State the importance of 'Prey-predator' relationship in a habitat.

When Plasmodium sp. (malarial parasite) enters the human body, it reproduces asexually and increases its number. During this course, the affected person suffers from malaria. After a number of asexual cycles, the parasite, in order to complete its life cycle, enters the sexual phase of its life. Trace the sexual stages in the life cycle of Plasmodium in a female Anopheles mosquito, when it bites an infected person, up to the formation of mature infective stages of the parasite.

(a) Name and state the type of immunity that acts as a 'biological shield' to the developing foetus against many infections in the mother's womb.
(b) A large proportion of infants remain free from potent infections at least three months after birth, or even longer if breast fed. Explain, giving suitable reasons.

With the advent of sophisticated techniques of genetic engineering, we can now readily purify and isolate DNA. Name and explain the different steps involved in the separation and isolation of DNA fragments once cut by restriction endonucleases.
"Some species in an ecosystem exert greater influence in driving major ecosystem services than others." How did Paul Ehrlich explain this concept in his 'rivet popper hypothesis' ?

(i) How has the introduction of Nile Perch into Lake Victoria in East Africa had a devastating effect on the indigenous species in the lake ?
(ii) Name two invasive weed species which have posed a threat to the existence of our native species.

Given below is a picture of a natural large habitat that is being continuously broken into smaller patches. This process is continuing, increasing and expanding over time due to human impact, thereby posing a great risk to the existence of species in the habitat.
(a) Do you agree with the above statement ? Give two suitable reasons in support of your answer.
(b) Write the ecological term used for such patches formed in an original habitat.
questions._figure: ILLUSTRATIVE: three sketched panels joined by arrows, from an 'Original Habitat' densely filled with trees, to a panel with fewer clumps of trees and 'Gaps', to a panel of isolated tree clumps with a label 'Gaps created over time due to human activities'; caption 'Habitat loss due to creation of 'patches' in a habitat'. The stem states everything the drawing shows, so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 8.

questions.stem: An application of biotechnology in agriculture involves production of pest resistant plants using 'cry' genes from a bacterium. Name the bacterium. Explain why the 'cry' gene kills the pest but not the bacterium itself.

questions.context: Development of recombinant DNA technology has opened gates to many breakthroughs in the fields of medicine and agriculture. This has enabled scientists to isolate, sequence and manipulate individual genes obtained from diverse living or dead cells. Given below is a diagram showing the basic steps involved in genetically modifying an organism. Study the given diagram and answer the questions that follow :
questions.stem: Are two different types of restriction endonucleases used, one to cut the vector DNA and another to cut the desired DNA to be cloned ? Support your answer, giving reason.
questions._figure: ILLUSTRATIVE: the case study's flow diagram: (1) Restriction Enzyme acting on a dark bar labelled (Gene of Interest) and (2) Restriction Enzyme acting on a ring labelled Plasmid (Vector); the two are bracketed and joined by an arrow marked (X) to (3) a ring with a dark insert labelled rDNA (vector); an arrow to (4) a cell labelled E. coli containing rings; four arrows to (5) four such cells, the group labelled (Y). This sub-part is answerable without it. Page idx 10.

questions.context:
RNA interference (RNAi) holds great potential as a therapeutic agent for the treatment of human diseases and as a bicontrol agent for controlling pests in the agricultural fields. An experiment was conducted to study the use of 'RNAi' for the potential treatment of disorders of cholesterol metabolism. Some people possess genetic mutations with elevated levels of 'ApoB' gene which predisposes them to coronary artery diseases.

Lowering the amount of 'ApoB' can reduce the number of lipoproteins and lower the blood cholesterol.

Tracy Zimmerman and her colleagues used RNAi in 2006 to reduce the level of 'ApoB' in non-human primates Cynomolgus monkeys. (i) One group of monkeys were given RNAi treatment (Small interfering RNAs, SiRNAs) (doses 1 mg/kg SiRNAs), (ii) Second group of monkeys were given RNAi treatment (doses \(2{\cdot}5\) mg/kg SiRNAs), and (iii) Third group of monkeys were injected saline as control .

The results of the experiments are illustrated in the graph given below :
questions.stem:
(i) What do you interpret from the bars (X and Z) obtained after 264 hours of treatment of monkeys with saline and \(2{\cdot}5\) mg/kg SiRNAs treatment ?
(ii) Name the category of organisms in the living world, where RNA interference (RNAi) takes place. Why ?
(iii) What is the basic principle involved in RNA interference (RNAi) in silencing the preferred genes ?
questions._figure: REQUIRED: a bar graph of Relative serum cholesterol (% per dose) (y, 0 to 120 in steps of 20) against Time (hours) at 24, 48, 144 and 264 (x), with three bars at each time keyed Saline X (cross-hatched), 1 mg/kg Y (vertical wavy lines) and \(2{\cdot}5\) mg/kg Z (solid black). The bar heights, and so how X and Z change by 264 hours, are what part (i) asks the student to interpret, so they are withheld here. Page idx 12.
